1:
Keil and Delitzsch set out the plan of the chapter first. It contains three words of God, connected in substance and design: the blood-guiltiness of the city, which hastens the day when it shall be an object of scorn to the whole world; the house of Israel become dross and about to be melted in the fire of tribulation; and the corruption of every rank, prophets, priests, princes and people, on account of which the judgment has burst upon them.

Henry stages the opening as a trial. The prophet sits as judge by commission from Heaven, and the city holds up her hand as a prisoner at the bar; if prophets were set over other nations, he says, much more over the nation of God. She is called the bloody city not merely for shedding blood but because her crimes in general were bloody, polluting her in her own blood and deserving that blood should be given her to drink. The business of a judge is to convict and then to pass sentence, and these are the two things the prophet is set to do; Henry calls the indictment a true bill, since the judgment written upon it is according to truth, and the showing of all her abominations is so that God may be justified in the desolations he brings.

On the murders Henry is specific. Blood was shed not only in the suburbs where the strangers lived but in the midst of the city, where one would think the magistrates would be vigilant; men were killed in duels, by secret assassination, or in the courts of justice under colour of law, and no care was taken to punish the murderers.

The doubled question at the head of the charge is handled three ways. Gill offers two senses, either that the prophet is asked whether he will plead for and excuse such a city, or whether he has courage enough to do his office and condemn her. Ellicott closes off the first, saying the marginal sense of pleading for is not appropriate here. Wesley takes the repetition as directed at the prophet rather than the city, doubled to awaken him and quicken him to his work.

The clause about her time coming draws the sharpest note. Ellicott points out that what will be the inevitable consequence of her acts is represented, by a very common figure, as though it had been her purpose in doing them; she had been so fully warned that persistence in the same course looks like a design to bring it on. Clarke reaches a similar place, that she has completed the time of her probation and grown daily worse, so that judgment can linger no longer. Wesley calls it the time of ripeness in her sins.

On the days and years Ellicott reports that the Rabbinical commentators distinguish them, the days meaning the destruction of the city and the years the captivity; Wesley says she is grown up to the eldest years in sin, beyond which she is not to go. Ellicott treats the mockery as a permanent principle, the necessary result in every age of the contrast between high professions and inconsistent performance. Their law, he says, stood far above the legislation of any nation, while the habitual conduct of the people was in utter disregard of it, and the effect was the one Paul described when he said the name of God was blasphemed among the Gentiles on their account. What exposed them peculiarly was the claim, as a chosen people, to a universal and everlasting dominion, set against their actual overthrow. Gill names the mockers, near and distant alike, and Clarke observes that through her many others had been drawn into ruin. Ellicott would drop the supplied words in the last clause and takes the phrase rendered much vexed of the internal confusion and social disorder that marked the decaying kingdom.
6:
Ellicott begins the catalogue with a correction of the rendering. The tense here matches the verbs that follow and both should be translated alike, and the word order altered, so that the sense is that the princes of Israel, every one according to his power, have been in her to shed blood. The charge is then plain: the rulers who should have preserved order and administered justice were themselves foremost in deeds of violence. Clarke reduces it to a proverb, like people, like prince, and Wesley observes that not one of a more merciful temper was to be found, each acting to the limit of his ability.

Gill takes the following verse as still concerning those princes; the children of the nobles are meant, and the sons and daughters of the king, from whom better might have been expected given their station and education. He makes contempt of parents a sin of the first magnitude, and notes that even among the heathen it was reckoned next to contempt of God himself; and if it prevailed among these it prevailed among the lower ranks too, who are always influenced by such examples.

Ellicott reads the whole indictment as a list of breaches of particular commands: filial respect was among the most frequently enjoined precepts, the despising of holy things and the profaning of sabbaths were the constant subject of the warnings of the law, tale-bearers were prohibited by name, eating upon the mountains means joining in the idol sacrifices, the sins of lewdness are all specifically named. Then he identifies the hinge of the list: the phrase about having forgotten God is at once the root of all these sins and in itself the climax of them.

On the tale-carriers Gill offers a picture and two versions. The word suggests men who go from house to house as pedlars do with their wares, so that one version renders it merchants; or else men who go into the courts and bear false witness, while two other versions make them thieves. Clarke calls them witnesses who will swear anything where life is concerned, and Wesley informers who give false evidence for money.

Gill notices the grammar twice where the others pass on. On the uncovering of a father nakedness he observes that the verb stands in the singular though several versions read it plural, and infers that the crime was committed only by a few. On the adultery of the next verse he offers three renderings, that a man of note has committed it, since the vice prevailed among the princes, or that every one has, the sin being general through every rank.

The bribes drawn for blood draw the sharpest distinction. Gill grants that to take bribes in matters of money is very wicked, but holds that to take them in cases which affect life is dreadfully cruel, whether the money buys a corrupt sentence from the bench or false evidence from a witness. Of the smiting of the hand Gill lists four senses, amazement, indignation, grief, or rejoicing at the punishment to come; Wesley takes it flatly as a testimony of abhorrence.

The close of the first prophecy turns on a single word. Ellicott would render it rather that they shall be profaned by themselves, noting that the word admits either sense according to its derivation; through their own misconduct they forfeit the privileges of a holy nation and become dishonoured in the sight of the heathen. Gill keeps the received sense, that they are no longer the inheritance of God but their own, which is a poor portion. Wesley turns the same reading into a taunt, that God was their inheritance while they obeyed, and that they may now be an inheritance to themselves if they can. Ellicott adds that this warning closes the first prophecy of the chapter and shows the extreme suffering necessary for the purification that follows.
17:
The second oracle turns on a figure from the refiner shop, and Ellicott explains why it was a favourite with the prophets. The completion of the refining of silver was determined by two signs, the parting of the floating dross and the appearance of the image of the refiner reflected from the molten surface. From it he draws the point that governs the whole section: the figure, while it sets out the punishment of Israel, shows clearly that the punishment was for the purpose of purification. Keil and Delitzsch connect the figure backwards, holding that this second word of God rests upon the language about the uncleanness of sin in the verse before it.

Henry works the metals one by one and turns each into a vice. The state had been a head of gold in the earlier reigns and arms of silver after the kingdoms divided; now it has degenerated into baser metal. Brass denotes the impudence of those who cannot blush; tin the hypocritical profession of piety that covers iniquity, a specious show without intrinsic worth; iron the cruel disposition of some and their delight in war; lead the dulness of men soft and pliable to evil yet too heavy to be moved toward good. He exclaims over the change, that the gold has become dross; and then he refuses even that much credit, since brass and tin and iron and lead, though of less value than silver, are at least of good use, whereas what is charged here is that the house of Israel has become dross.

Gill sharpens the charge by adding to whom they are dross. Among themselves they might still be reckoned silver, and formerly they had been so; but to God, who searches the heart and knows the spring of every action, they appeared as dross. Wesley finds the failure of the earlier discipline in the word: the afflictions already laid on them had not bettered them, and while they loved mercy and did justly they were as silver, whereas now they are only dross. Clarke draws the consequence: they must be put into the furnace and subjected to the most intense fire until the impurities are consumed, since no ordinary means will avail and the most violent must be resorted to.

Why the city itself should be the crucible Ellicott answers from geography and history together: it is the refining pot into which the people are cast because it was at once their national centre and the centre of the war by which they were carried away. Clarke fills in the mechanics, that the whole people are gathered into the pot and the fire of the invaders is to melt them, and that as a refiner blows his fire with the bellows so God will blow upon them with the fire of his wrath. Wesley adds the means, that a secret overruling providence would bring them into the city as into a furnace. Gill emphasises how general the corruption was, king and princes and nobles and prophets and priests as well as the common people, with scarcely an exception in city or country.

Gill makes two observations on the list of metals that the others let pass. The first is technical, that refiners do not gather the several metals together as the verse describes but treat each apart. The second is more serious: silver is named among the things gathered into the furnace, which he takes to mean that those who were truly good should suffer in the same calamity, tried and purified by it rather than exempted. Ellicott corrects one clause in the same verse, rendering it not that God will leave them there but that he will cast them in; and Gill notes at the end that the burning was not only figurative, since the city and the temple were in the event burnt with material fire.
23:
Ellicott marks the third and last communication here, a further enumeration of the sins, committed by all classes alike, ending like the other two with the outpouring of wrath. On the opening description he reports much difference of opinion, and gives as most probable a reading drawn from husbandry: the land is neglected, the stones not gathered up and the weeds allowed to grow, so that it has had neither human care nor the divine blessing of rain. Clarke keeps to the weather, a country where no rain falls to cleanse the garments or fertilise the ground.

Henry canvasses four senses and chooses none. The land may be said not to be cleansed as metal is refined, and so to need the furnace again; or the rain withheld may be the teaching of the prophets, whose doctrine is said to descend as rain; or the sense may be that when corrected she was not cleansed, her filth not carried away as a street is by a sweeping rain; or the want may be of comfort rather than cleansing, nothing to refresh her in the day of indignation. Wesley combines two, that the judgments had been as violent floods and hottest fires and yet had carried away neither her filth nor her dross.

Henry states the principle of the indictment. The charge is drawn against the several orders of men, and shows that all had helped to fill the measure of the guilt while none had done anything toward emptying it; every one had corrupted his own way, and those who should have been the brightest examples of virtue were the ringleaders in iniquity.

On the first order Ellicott is the fullest. The opposition of false prophets to the measures taken for the reformation of the people is continually spoken of as among the most serious obstacles to the true prophets. His observation is that nothing could have furnished a more plausible excuse for disobeying an admonition than an opposing claim to speak in the name of the Lord; and the greed of these men and the effects of their counsel are set out here in stronger terms than in any other passage. Clarke reads the conspiracy as a compact to say and support the same things. Wesley makes the contrivance more particular, an agreement to speak alike in smooth words, the treasure taken as the reward of their lies and the widows made by persuading the king to hold out the war. Gill insists only on whose prophets they were, not the Lord own but hers.

The priests come next in influence, and Ellicott states their trust: it was their office to observe and teach the distinction between the holy and the unholy and to care for the sabbath, and in every part they had been unfaithful. Gill takes the charge of violating the law in the sense of forcing it, since they wrested its meaning and broke themselves what they were appointed to teach. Clarke observes that men whose lips should preserve knowledge had not instructed the people, and had violated the law in their manner of serving in the temple. Wesley divides the failure three ways, that they neither differenced the holy from the profane in practice, nor taught the difference, nor separated the one from the other in the exercise of their authority.

Ellicott takes the princes to mean not the kings only but the nobles and those in authority at court, whose injustice is a constant theme of prophetic rebuke. Gill turns the figure against their office, since men of the first rank ought to have protected the meaner sort and were instead cruel, preying on the harmless as wolves prey on lambs. Clarke makes them no better than the priests, and Wesley reads the destroying of souls as the ruin of families, the fathers cut off and the widow and fatherless impoverished.
28:
The prophets are brought back a second time, and Ellicott explains why: they are named again for their powerful influence upon the princes, whom they led astray by falsehoods; and he glosses the phrase about seeing vanity as an expression for pretended and false visions. Gill takes the daubing very concretely, that they palliated the sins of the rulers and declared it right to shed the blood they had shed and to seize the estates of men. That, he grants, might satisfy the consciences of the princes for a while and stop the clamour of the people against them; but it would not last, being like a wall built of bad stuff which will not stand and then daubed with mortar that soon washes off. Clarke says the same of their pretensions, that men professing to be prophets soothed the people in their sins and claimed oracles of peace where nothing had been spoken to them; and Wesley calls it flattery, promises which, like ill-tempered mortar, will deceive in the end though everything looks smooth now.

The last class is the people themselves. Ellicott defines them simply as the common people, not belonging to any of the orders already named. Gill narrows it to the more powerful among them, those in greatest authority in cities and towns and families, who oppressed the poor and those under them, their servants and tenants, men not able to defend themselves; and he notes that two versions read the verse instead of the prophets using the people ill. Clarke states it as a rule that holds through the whole chapter, that all who had power or authority had abused it, and vexed the poor and the needy and the stranger.

The search for a man in the gap is handled with unusual care, because taken flatly it would say too much. Gill sets the limit first: the search was among the princes, priests, prophets and people just described, for otherwise there were certainly good men in the land, and he names two of them; the point is that none was found among these. Ellicott makes the same qualification on other grounds. He treats the making up of the hedge as only another form of standing in the gap, added for emphasis, both referring to intercession for the people; and from that he concludes that it is not meant that there was not a single godly man, but that there was not one of such pure, strong and commanding character that his intercession might avert the threatened doom.

Wesley guards the sentence in a different way, by observing that God is speaking after the manner of men, and takes the man sought as any one at all, from among princes or prophets or priests or people, who might repair the breach; the standing in the gap he explains as interposing between a sinful people and their offended God and entreating for mercy. Clarke gives the office more content still. He reads the breach as one made in the moral state and feeling of the people, and the man sought as one who would faithfully exhort, reprove and counsel with all long-suffering and doctrine; and he ends the sentence as the verse does, that none was to be found.

Clarke closes the chapter by gathering the whole indictment into a single question. Because of the profligacy, the false worship so generally practised, the false prophets tolerated, the unholy and profane priesthood, the oppressive princes, the deceiving prophets, the oppressions of petty officers, and the total corruption of manners in every rank and office, he asks whether there has not been sufficient reason for abandoning such a people and pouring out upon them so destructive a storm. Gill puts the same conclusion in an image, that the indignation came like a mighty torrent, carrying all before it.
